Biggest mistake first, and it isn't strike selection or any of the stuff people argue about. It's when you sell them.  Premium comes from implied volatility. Sell into a calm market and you're taking on the same obligation for a fraction of the pay.  Sell into fear and it's 2 or 3x for the identical strike on the identical company.  If a name has been drifting sideways for a month there's usually nothing worth selling and I just leave it alone.  1️⃣ Close at 50%  This one annoyed me when I first worked it out, because it's so obvious in hindsight.  Say you sell a put for $200 with 35 days on it. 10 days in, it's worth $100. You've collected half the premium in under a third of the time.  Hold to expiry and you're at roughly 24% annualized. Close at 50% on day 10 and start again, you're at 47%.  The back half of that premium is the slowest money you will ever collect, and you're carrying assignment risk the entire time you sit there waiting for it.  Just take the easy half.  2️⃣ Roll for a credit or don't roll at all  Stock drops and you're not ready for assignment. You can buy your put back and sell a lower strike further out.  If the new premium covers what it costs to close plus something extra, that's a credit. Better strike, more time, and you got paid to do it.  If it costs you money to roll, don't. Take the shares. That was always the plan.  I've watched people roll at a debit 3 or 4 times in a row trying to avoid assignment on a stock they told everyone they wanted to own. Makes no sense.  3️⃣ Your collateral shouldn't be sitting in cash  $9,500 in T-bills or a money market earns around $34 over a 35 day trade at current rates.  Against a $200 premium that's 17% more income for doing nothing at all.  Small on its own. Adds up over a year.  4️⃣ Ladder it  Don't stack everything on one strike and one expiry.  Spread the dates out so something is always coming off, cash is always freeing up, and one bad week doesn't land on your entire book at once.  5️⃣ Size the book, not the trade  This is the one that actually hurts people.  5 puts open, market drops 12%, and you don't get assigned on one of them. You get assigned on all five, same day, and you need every dollar at the same time.  Before you open anything, ask whether you'd be genuinely fine owning every single position at full size tomorrow morning. If the answer is no, you're already too big and you just haven't found out yet.  6️⃣ The wheel  You got assigned. Fine. Sell a covered call above your cost basis.  Called away and you're back in cash with two lots of premium plus the gain. Not called away, you keep the premium and go again next month.  7️⃣ Only on companies you've already done the work on  The premium is the bonus for waiting. It's never the reason.  Any time the yield is the most interesting thing about a trade, that's usually the market pricing in something you haven't looked at properly yet.  Every premium you collect can go straight back into collateral. More collateral means bigger premiums means more collateral.  Run that for a few years and the income is no longer pocket money. The Clarity Act.  The Banking Lobby’s False Crypto Alarm  The banking lobby’s argument against the CLARITY Act rests on a catchy but false premise: that clearer rules for digital assets will somehow “kill banks.”   The data say otherwise. American banking is consolidating, but crypto is not the culprit. The number of banks has fallen for decades because of mergers, low new-bank formation, expensive technology, regulatory fixed costs, and the enormous scale advantages enjoyed by JPMorgan Chase and other national giants. From 2020 to 2025, the number of U.S. banks fell 13 percent while average assets per bank rose 33 percent. That is consolidation, not a cryptocurrency-induced death spiral.  Nor is crypto draining the banking system of deposits. Commercial-bank deposits fell after the Federal Reserve’s rate hikes made Treasury bills and money-market funds more attractive. But deposits have resumed growing; core deposits expanded about 4 percent in the first three quarters of 2025, against 1.5 percent in the same period a year earlier. Total commercial-bank deposits were roughly $19.4 trillion by mid-2026.  The banking lobby warns that stablecoin yield will pull deposits from traditional institutions. Yet dollar-linked stablecoins and related digital-asset platforms have offered rewards, rebates, and yield-like returns for years. Bank deposits nevertheless increased. That does not prove stablecoins pose no competitive risk. It does refute the claim that yield-bearing digital dollars have already triggered a systemic exodus from banks. More important, blockchain need not disintermediate banks at all.   Tokenized deposits are conventional bank deposits represented on blockchain rails: a direct claim on a regulated bank, held on its balance sheet, but capable of 24/7, programmable transfer and potentially instantaneous settlement. They preserve the deposit base, credit intermediation, and customer relationship while offering much of the utility that makes stablecoins attractive.  The CLARITY Act should be seen as pro-competition financial infrastructure. It can establish rules, deter fraud, require disclosure, and distinguish decentralized networks from securities offerings—while enabling regulated banks to custody digital assets, use tokenized deposits, and compete in onchain finance.  America does not save banks by shielding incumbent toll collectors from competition. It preserves financial leadership by allowing its banks to compete.

Guerin was a great value investor. During two decades around 1960s, he made a whopping 33% annualised returns when compared to index's annualised returns of 8.5%. His track record then was even superior to Buffett. You've no clue what 33% annualised returns for two decades means.  He became very close to Buffett and Munger and worked together with them. As we repeatedly tell now Buffett and Munger, earlier it used to be Buffett, Munger and Guerin.  Buffett wrote a famous essay, "The super investors of Graham and Dodsville" where he mentions Guerin as a top value investor.  A gut wrenching bear market happened in 1973-74, where the index lost a huge 45%.  Buffett and Munger decided to wait patiently. Guerin sensing a huge opportunity in that severe crash, borrowed heavily and invested in stocks. Buffett and Munger were heavily against borrowing money to invest in markets. Guerin's different approach started building strain in his relationship with Buffett and Munger.  To Guerin's misfortune, the stocks he purchased further fell down triggering margin calls. He has to completely dispose of his wealth at distressed prices to repay the debt. Guerin never completely recovered after that. He faded from public view in 1983.  He passed away in 2020. Various estimates suggest that Guerin would have been worth not less than few billion dollars had he not got into debt to invest in markets. Not only that his name would have now been etched as one of the greatest investors of all time, along with Buffett and Munger.  Later in life, Buffett said that "Rick was just as smart as us, but he was in a hurry."  As I mentioned the other day, even now Buffett keeps upto 30% of his portfolio in ultrasafe short term treasury bills. He once said, despite being richest in the world, he would have been many more times rich had he used borrowing to amplify his returns.   Guerin was one of the finest brains in investing. He completely disappeared from public memory because unfortunately his temperament did not match his intellect.  When such a tragedy can happen to a legend in investing, how much we should be careful with diversification, asset allocation, not borrowing to invest, being conservative, having safe money and so on.  Never chase only returns forgetting the risk. In investing, first you've to survive. Then only comes growth and compounding. Return of capital is as or more important than return on capital.

I haven’t talked about DeFi in a while, but the space looks very different now.  It is not just “farm this pool, chase that APY, rotate before emissions die” anymore.  The serious part of DeFi is slowly turning into a competition for flow.  Stablecoin flow. Swap flow. Borrow flow. Leverage flow. Validator flow. Treasury flow. Collateral flow.  The projects that matter most are not always the ones with the loudest incentives.  They are usually the ones sitting closest to where money already moves.  That is how I look at DeFi now.  Not as one big category.  More like 7 different flow businesses.  1⃣ Stablecoin flow  This is still the center of everything.  @Tether_to and @circle are the obvious giants because USDT and USDC are still the main settlement assets across crypto.  People trade with them. Borrow against them. LP with them. Bridge them. Hold them on exchanges. Use them as margin. Use them as dry powder.  Then you have newer onchain dollar systems like @SkyEcosystem, @ethena_labs, PYUSD, USDS, USDe, GHO, RLUSD, USDG and others fighting for a different part of the stack.  This is where things get interesting.  A stablecoin is not just a stablecoin anymore.  Some are backed by reserves. Some are backed by crypto collateral. Some are powered by protocol revenue. Some use basis and funding. Some are tied to T-bills and money markets. Some are designed for payments. Some are designed for DeFi composability.  Same $1 target.  Very different engine under the hood.  That is why stablecoins are probably the most important DeFi product category, even though people treat them as boring.  Boring is usually where size goes first.  2⃣ Borrow flow  This is where @aave still feels like the main character. Aave is not just a lending app anymore. It is becoming a liquidity layer for collateral and credit.  The important thing about Aave V4 is not “new version number.”  It is the Hub and Spoke idea.  Shared liquidity sits in hubs. Different borrowing environments plug into it. Risk can be separated without fragmenting liquidity everywhere.  That is a big deal because lending markets always fight the same problem: how do you increase capital efficiency without letting one bad collateral type poison the whole system? Then you have @Morpho, which attacks the same market from a different angle.  Morpho feels more like lending infrastructure.  Permissionless markets. Curated vaults. Risk caps. Adapters. Different managers building different vault strategies on top.  That makes Morpho less like “one lending market” and more like a marketplace for credit risk.  @compoundfinance is still one of the OGs. @sparkdotfi sits close to the Sky/Maker credit system. @0xfluid is interesting because it mixes lending, liquidity and DEX design into one capital efficiency thesis.  The lesson here is simple:  lending protocols win when they become the default place where collateral wants to sit.  Not when they temporarily show the highest APY.  3⃣ Swap flow  This is the part most people understand, but still underestimate.  @Uniswap is still the default mental model for AMMs.  But Uniswap v4 changes the conversation because hooks let pools become more programmable.  Dynamic fees. Custom pool logic. Permissioned pools. Lending hooks. Different ways to route and manage liquidity.  That means the future of AMMs is not just “who has the deepest ETH/USDC pool?”  It becomes:  who can attract the best liquidity design?  Then you have @pancakefi doing huge cross-chain volume, @aeroxyz acting like the liquidity hub for Base, @CurveFinance still owning a very specific stable/pegged asset niche, and Solana names like @JupiterExchange, @orca_so, @RaydiumProtocol and @MeteoraAG competing for very fast retail flow. This is why DEXs are hard to analyze.  TVL alone is not enough.  Volume matters. Routing matters. Fee capture matters. LP profitability matters. Chain growth matters. Frontend distribution matters. Incentive efficiency matters.  A DEX with sticky flow is a toll road.  A DEX with rented flow is just a campaign.  4⃣ Leverage flow  This is where @HyperliquidX changed the standard. A few years ago, perps were mostly a CEX product with some onchain alternatives. Now onchain perps are one of the most important parts of DeFi. Hyperliquid proved that people will use onchain venues if the product is fast enough, liquid enough, and simple enough.  That matters because perp venues own some of the best flow in crypto:  active traders, liquidations, funding, maker/taker fees, open interest, and constant volatility.  @dYdX is still important. @GMX_IO pioneered a lot of the perp LP vault thinking. @DriftProtocol and Jupiter Perps are important on Solana. Newer venues will keep showing up because leverage is one of crypto’s most natural products.  But this category has one big trap.  People call it yield.  Sometimes it is actually market making risk.  If you deposit into a perp LP or dealer vault, you are not just “earning passive APY.”  You are often taking the other side of traders, funding, liquidations, or inventory risk.  That can be great.  But only if you understand when the house can bleed.  5⃣ Validator flow  This is the most underrated boring bucket. @LidoFinance made stETH one of the most important collateral assets in Ethereum DeFi.  The reason is simple:  staked ETH becomes liquid. That liquid asset becomes usable in lending markets, LPs, vaults, structured products, and collateral loops.  So Lido is not just a staking protocol.  It is collateral infrastructure.  @jito_sol plays a similar role on Solana, with staking and MEV sitting close to the chain’s economic activity.  @Rocket_Pool matters from a decentralization angle. @ether_fi and restaking products added another layer by turning staked ETH into security marketplace exposure.  The interesting part is that validator yield is one of the few native crypto yields that does not need a points campaign to exist.  But it still has real risks.  Validator risk. Slashing risk. Withdrawal liquidity. Wrapper risk. Depeg risk. Operator concentration. Extra complexity from restaking.  Staking is boring until it becomes the base asset for everything else.  6⃣ Treasury flow  This is where RWA finally became hard to ignore.  @BlackRock BUIDL through Securitize, @OndoFinance, @SuperstateFunds, @MapleFinance, Spiko, Franklin’s BENJI, OpenEden and others are not trying to look like old DeFi farms.  They are trying to bring treasury-style yield, money market exposure, credit products, and tokenized funds onchain.  This bucket is important because it speaks a language bigger capital understands.  Collateral. Duration. Redemption. Custody. Legal structure. Issuer risk. Credit risk. Transparency. Transfer restrictions. Distribution.  The funny thing is that RWA yield can look less exciting than a farm, but it can absorb far more capital.  A tiny LP opportunity dies when everyone finds it.  T-bills and money markets do not care about your CT thread.  That is why RWA is probably not a “hot narrative” anymore.  It is becoming part of the balance sheet layer.  7⃣ Router flow  This is the category I think more people should watch.  The winners might not only be protocols that create yield or liquidity.  They might be interfaces that route users into everything.  @JupiterExchange on Solana is a good example.  Swap, perps, lend, portfolio, routing, execution.  The more products live behind one interface, the more user flow gets captured at the front door.  Uniswap is moving in this direction too with app, wallet, routing, v4, hooks, Unichain and now embedded earn products.  Aave Pro is also interesting because lending becomes easier to manage once users can see risk, hubs, spokes, health factor and rate data in one place.  This matters because DeFi has a UX problem. Most users do not want 19 tabs open.  They want one place that tells them:  where can I swap? where can I borrow? where can I earn? where can I manage risk? where can I exit?  The protocol with the best product surface can capture value even if the underlying strategy is built somewhere else.  That is the part many people miss.  DeFi is not only about who builds the deepest pool anymore.  It is also about who owns the user relationship.  So my DeFi checklist changed.  I used to ask:  What is the APY? What is the token incentive? Is there an airdrop? How early is this farm?  Now I ask:  Does this protocol own real flow? Is that flow organic or rented? Can the protocol keep users without incentives? Does it make money when users are active? Does liquidity get deeper as usage grows? Is the asset useful as collateral somewhere else? Can other protocols build on top of it? Can size enter without destroying the trade? What risk am I taking if everyone exits at once?  That framework makes the space much easier to read.  Aave owns borrow flow.  Uniswap owns swap flow. Lido owns validator collateral flow.  Hyperliquid owns leverage flow.  Tether and Circle own dollar flow.  Sky and Ethena are competing for productive dollar flow.  Morpho owns curated credit flow. Aerodrome owns a big piece of Base liquidity flow.  Jupiter owns Solana routing flow.  Ondo, Securitize, Superstate and Maple are fighting for treasury and credit flow.  Different products. Same question: where does capital naturally want to move? That is the real DeFi game now. Not chasing the highest number on a dashboard. Finding the protocols that become harder to avoid as the market grows. Because the best DeFi projects do not just offer yield.  They become financial roads.  And every time someone swaps, borrows, stakes, hedges, lends, loops, bridges, deposits, or exits…  they pay the toll.

I think that EIP 8361 tries to do too many things (increasing the moneyness of ETH, pre-empting remotely possible future decreases security due to overstake, protecting solo stakers, etc) at once and in my estimation will mostly do the opposite. I honestly believe that issuance change is too complicated to treat with this urgency, that the far-future concerns are drastically overblown, and it's very bad timing to introduce such a divisive proposal, especially in such a way. It has also been pushed last minute in an attempt to squeeze into Hegota (still subject to the EIP Inclusion process), even though potential issuance changes had been communicated as per the current strawmap to be slated for I* at the earliest. IMO, this proposal lays Ethereum's hard-fought uniqueness (real decentralization and neutrality) at the sacrificial altar of ETH as money, camouflaged against an insufficiently scrutinized concept of "minimally viable" security spend. Unfortunately, it also doesn't come to terms with the fact the moral hazard of a "too big to fail" event is not necessarily mitigated by limiting staking adoption, only displaced, as ETH seeking yield will mostly just go to more risky and likely custodial solutions, in my estimation thereby increasing the likelihood of such an event.  Apart from misgivings around the governance and consensus (or lack thereof, given its wide-reaching scope and implications) process around this proposal, I find that the selective supporting research is too theoretical and is lacking from a macro, micro and behavioral economic modeling perspective, especially with regards to 2nd and 3rd order effects. This applies to especially to two aspects:  1) one of the central theses around the urgent concern about the stake rate (which is lower than most other PoS networks which are mostly fine) that also hinges on the idea that just because issuance is positive at 100% stake then there's necessarily incentive to do so (ignoring years of economic history and literature which illustrate that demand is actually expressed as a complex function of utility, and not merely purely theoretic expected value, and strong contra examples such as USD as cash/savings vs T-Bills); and  2) on the effect of drastically reduced issuance (and real validator rewards) on the resulting validator set, and the negative externalities that will be born out of this material change in monetary policy (and possible further changes which might be required for correction).   Due to the new proposed curve a very real possibility of a sustained equilibrium at or near 50% of Ethereum staked with 0 nominal (nevermind real) yield is now possible, which would essentially be a death-knell for the security of the network, as node operators and staking protocols which prioritize expertise, decentralization, and expensive know-how are priced out and large, centralized, minimal-cost parties take over the operation of the overwhelming majority of the network's validators. Unfortunately, at current ETH/USD prices, such a scenario isn't even necessary for this proposed issuance change to lead to a large consolidation of the operator set, which would drastically lower the network's Nakamoto coefficient and thus its resilience.  In an eventuality where few actors are allowed to control one of the fundamental levers of the network -- determining its security (i.e. control of fork choice) -- by simply being able to offer staking at break-even or at a loss for long enough to price most other actors out of the market, what will be left of Ethereum's neutrality when the only recourse (now made ever-more necessary) will be a substantial and messy social slashing? Not much.  I'm not against an issuance reduction in general; I am against an issuance reduction without centering on the core questions, and giving the community adequate time, tools, and analysis to be able to consider the bevy of implications. To me these core questions are: * What is the right amount of economic security given that we want Ethereum to be the centerpiece of onchain finance? A minimum viable security approach here doesn't cut it -- nation states don't think this way and the largest financial network in the world shouldn't either * What is the effect of the market structures generated by any issuance curve, the relevant expected prices of operation (eg in ETH/fiat terms), and the effect of issuance changes -- and their consequences -- on demand for the asset, especially on the underlying validator and node operator set? * How does the network retain its neutrality, utility, and demand, if social slashing is utilized not in the same way that nuclear arms are (as a last-measure deterrent) but rather as as the go-to solution for problems created by the network's own security paradigm? * Why do we honestly believe that the terminal staking rate is in the high double digits? What practical economic modelling or historical indicators are there to point towards this? * Are we okay with a hyper-centralized validator set just because if they misbehave we will socially slash them? Why have PoS at all then and not just go to PoA or PoG?

🤔The United States has two kinds of dollars.  The first kind is the one in your bank account. That's not actually government money it's a promise from your bank that they'll give you government money if you ask. Your bank created it when they made a loan or took a deposit. It sits on their books, not the government's.  The second kind is the one the Federal Reserve issues physical cash, and the reserves that banks hold at the Fed. That is government money. A direct liability of the United States.  For most of history, that distinction didn't matter much. Your bank dollar and a Fed dollar spent the same. But digital technology made a third option possible: a central bank digital currency a digital dollar issued directly by the Fed, held directly by you, no bank in the middle.  Most major countries are building one. China has one running. Europe is designing one. The idea is straightforward: if money is going digital anyway, maybe the government should issue the digital version itself rather than letting private companies do it.  The United States just passed a law saying no.  In June 2026, Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. It's a 374-page housing bill. Buried in the last pages Title XI, Section 1101 is a provision that prohibits the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency through December 31, 2030. The Senate passed it 85 to 5. The House cleared it the next day.  The Fed cannot issue one. Cannot create one. Cannot have a bank create one on its behalf. Until at least 2031  and even then, only if Congress affirmatively says yes.  So who does get to make digital dollars?  Private companies. Under the GENIUS Act, signed into law in July 2025, private stablecoins digital tokens pegged one-to-one to the U.S. dollar and backed by Treasury bills are now regulated by banking agencies like the OCC, not by the SEC. Companies like Circle, Tether, Paxos, and others can issue them. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is granting trust bank charters to stablecoin issuers right now. At least eight applications are in the pipeline.  The law that regulates private digital dollars passed first. The law that bans the government's digital dollar passed second. Together they create a very specific structure:  Private companies build the digital dollar. The central bank is prohibited from competing.  The bill's drafters even wrote in a carve-out making sure private stablecoins aren't accidentally caught by the ban. Any dollar-denominated currency that is "open, permissionless, and private" is explicitly exempt.  Why this matters, explained simply.  Before 1951, the Federal Reserve did what the Treasury told it to do. Interest rates, bond purchases, monetary policy  Treasury called the shots. In 1951, the Fed and Treasury signed an agreement called the Accord, and the Fed became independent. For the next 75 years, the Fed set interest rates, regulated banks, and was the most powerful financial institution in the country.  What's been happening since roughly 2017, and accelerating since 2025, is that the Fed's role has been narrowing back down. Not by one dramatic announcement by a series of quiet, specific exclusions:  The Fed was not included when the stablecoin rules were written. The Fed was not included when the joint crypto rulemaking was proposed. The Fed did not participate when two other banking regulators asked a court to vacate their own consumer-protection rule. And now the Fed has been prohibited by statute from issuing a digital dollar.  Meanwhile, Treasury's enforcement arm FinCEN, OFAC, the sanctions apparatus  is expanding. Record penalties. New authorities. More tools.  The Fed still sets interest rates. That hasn't changed. But every other domain digital currency, financial enforcement, crypto oversight, stablecoin regulation is moving to Treasury or to Treasury-supervised private institutions.  The pattern isn't "the Fed is being attacked." The pattern is "the Fed is being reduced to rates."  @Homeranger17 @drawandstrike @CouchGuy17

The economics of this Housing Levy story deserves far more scrutiny.  The government reportedly invested Sh46 billion of Housing Levy collections in Treasury Bills. Treasury Bills do not sit there for decoration. They earn interest.  So let us do basic economics:  If Sh46 billion of workers’ and employers’ money was invested to generate returns, the principal is not the only public resource that must be accounted for. The interest is public money too.  Where is it?  How much interest accrued?  Was it reinvested?  Was it transferred to the Affordable Housing Fund?  Was it spent elsewhere?  If it was spent, on what authority and for what purpose?  This is where public finance gets interesting. Government should not be allowed to collect a compulsory levy, invest the idle balances, earn income from that money, and then only report the original amount as though the investment returns disappeared into thin air.  Imagine giving your SACCO manager Sh1 million to hold for you. He invests it, earns Sh100,000 in interest, then returns to you and proudly announces:  "Your Sh1 million has been used." Naturally, you would ask: What happened to the Sh100,000? That is the question Kenyans should be asking. The Housing Levy was deducted compulsorily from workers and matched by employers. Every shilling collected has an owner: the Kenyan public. Therefore, every return generated from those funds must be transparently recorded, disclosed and subjected to public accountability.  This is not a small accounting footnote. Interest income is part of the economic value generated by public funds. Until the government provides a clear reconciliation of the Sh46 billion principal, the interest earned, where that interest was credited, and how it was eventually applied, the numbers remain incomplete.  Public finance is not just about tracking the money you collect. It is also about tracking the money that money makes.  Where did the interest go?

Retiring UPDF Officers Tipped on Prudent Financial Management Ahead of Retirement.  6 August 2026  Senior Officers of the Uganda Peoples' Defence Forces (UPDF) who are due for retirement have been challenged to strengthen their financial management skills and plan wisely for life after military service to ensure long-term financial stability.  The call was made during a financial literacy training for retiring senior officers held at the Defence Intelligence and Security Headquarters in Mbuya. The training brought together facilitators from the Bank of Uganda and Britam, who were invited to equip the officers with financial literacy skills to ease their transition into retirement.  The Joint Staff Human Resource Management, Major General James Kinalwa, urged the officers to maintain a steady financial flow after retirement and avoid disposing of their assets due to poor financial planning.  "You have been used to a monthly salary, subsistence allowances, office benefits and out-of-pocket facilitation, which may no longer be available once you leave the army," Maj Gen Kinalwa said.  He encouraged the officers to make prudent financial decisions and invest wisely to secure their future after leaving active service.  Mr Hashim Kirungi, from the Bank of Uganda, described financial literacy as an essential life skill that everyone should acquire.  He urged the officers to reassess their financial habits by distinguishing between needs and wants, setting clear financial goals, and keeping track of both income and expenditure.  "It's never too late. This is the right time," Mr Kirungi said.  On savings, he advised the officers to prioritise saving before spending.  "Save first as soon as you earn because problems and demands are endless," he said, adding that savings provide the capital needed to establish sustainable businesses after retirement.  He cautioned the officers against borrowing money to start businesses, noting that such ventures carry significant risks and could result in financial losses.  Speaking on retirement planning, Mr Kirungi advised the officers to remain calm and make measured decisions once they receive their retirement packages.  "As soon as you get your package, take it easy," he said.  He also encouraged them to prioritise their health, family and personal relationships, noting that proper planning would enable them to enjoy a peaceful and fulfilling retirement.  Another Bank of Uganda facilitator, Mr Arnold Bagubwagye, delivered a presentation on investing in Treasury Bills, highlighting their benefits as a secure investment option for retirees.  Representing Britam, the Business Development Manager, Mr Ronald Mugabi, thanked the UPDF leadership for creating an opportunity to prepare retiring officers for life after service.  He encouraged the officers to set retirement goals using the SMART approach, ensuring that they are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.  "You have served your country and secured the nation. You should now focus on protecting what you have worked so hard to achieve," Mr Mugabi said.  Speaking on behalf of the retiring senior officers, Colonel Okei Rukogota commended the Chief of Defence Forces, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, and the UPDF leadership for organising the training and encouraged his colleagues to apply the knowledge gained to create wealth while maintaining healthy lifestyles through regular exercise.  The training was attended by retiring senior officers, officials from the Joint Staff Human Resource Management, and financial literacy facilitators from the Bank of Uganda and Britam.

A Trend-Following Strategy (18% Annual Returns Since 1926)  A recent research paper, “A Century of Profitable Industry Trends,” by Carlo Zarattini and Gary Antonacci demonstrates that a straightforward trend-following approach applied to industries has produced impressive long-term results.   The system, based on breakout entries, trailing exits, and volatility-adjusted position sizing, generated approximately 18% annualized returns going back to 1926 across 48 industry portfolios, while maintaining strong risk-adjusted performance.  Trading Rules  The strategy detects trends using simple breakout techniques. A long position is initiated whenever an industry’s closing price rises above the upper boundary of either a Donchian Channel or a Keltner Channel.  The Donchian signal uses the highest price observed during the previous 20 trading days, while the lower band relies on a longer 40-day lookback period. This asymmetry encourages the system to remain invested during sustained advances.   The Keltner Channel is constructed around a 20-day exponential moving average combined with a volatility buffer equal to 1.4 times the Average True Range, again paired with a 40-day lower band.  The strategy only takes long positions. When no industries display clear upward momentum, capital is allocated to Treasury bills instead of remaining exposed to equities.  Risk management  Risk management is handled through volatility targeting. Each industry position is scaled so that it contributes a similar amount of risk to the overall portfolio. Allocation weights are therefore inversely proportional to recent 14-day volatility, meaning more volatile industries receive smaller positions. To keep leverage within realistic limits, total portfolio exposure is capped at 200%.  Exits are governed by a trailing stop mechanism. The stop level is defined as whichever is higher between the lower Donchian band and the lower Keltner band, both calculated using a 40-day lookback. Importantly, once the stop moves higher, it is never reduced. This allows profitable trends to continue while ensuring losing trades are closed quickly.  Results (Backtested)  The industry trend-following approach achieved an annualized return of 18.2%, nearly twice the 9.7% return of the passive U.S. equity market over the same period. Risk-adjusted performance improved significantly as well, with a Sharpe ratio of 1.39 compared to 0.63 for the market benchmark.  The timing component also dramatically reduced drawdowns. Maximum losses were lowered by almost 60%, with the strategy experiencing a peak decline of about 33%, versus an 84% drawdown in equities. The return profile is clearly convex: the system participates strongly during rising markets, reflected in an upside beta of 1.16, while substantially limiting losses during downturns, with a downside beta of just 0.31.  A Practical ETF Implementation Since 2005  In the final section of the paper, Zarattini and Antonacci examine whether the strategy can be implemented realistically using exchange-traded funds.  This practical version covers the period from January 2005 through March 2024 and incorporates trading costs and real-world constraints to evaluate performance under modern market conditions.  Even after including estimated transaction costs of USD 0.0035 per trade, the ETF-based industry trend-following model delivered stronger risk-adjusted performance than passive exposure to the market through SPY.  The ETF implementation achieved a Sharpe ratio of 0.61, slightly exceeding the market’s 0.59. It also generated annual alpha of approximately 2.7% relative to the benchmark.  Risk reduction remained one of the most notable advantages. While the S&P 500 experienced a maximum drawdown of about 55%, the timing strategy limited losses to roughly 24%. With a beta of only 0.40, the system frequently held only the strongest sector ETFs, significantly lowering overall market exposure.  We strongly recommend reading the original research paper for a deeper understanding of the methodology and results.

Article about @The_DTCC and Tokenized Securities: What Changes in October 2026  In October, the institution at the center of American securities markets plans to give Wall Street a new way to move some of its most familiar assets. Shares in major companies, index funds and U.S. government debt will be eligible for a service that connects traditional custody with blockchain networks.   For banks and investment firms, that could change how securities are transferred, financed and used as collateral. For everyone watching the #tokenization story, October will offer something more concrete than another announcement: an opportunity to see whether the technology becomes part of everyday market operations.  The organization is the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation, or DTCC. Through its subsidiaries, it helps process the transactions that take place after investors agree to buy or sell securities. Its depository subsidiary, DTC, reported $114 trillion in securities under custody and servicing for 2025. Across DTCC's subsidiaries, annual securities transaction processing reached $4.7 quadrillion.   That enormous figure requires context. It measures transactions processed over a year, including repeated activity involving the same assets. It is not a pool of money scheduled to enter cryptocurrency markets. The October launch concerns a defined service for eligible securities, with adoption driven by participating firms.  The eligible universe includes Russell 1000 stocks, exchange-traded funds tracking major indexes, and U.S. Treasury bills, notes and bonds. Participation is voluntary. Firms will decide which eligible holdings to convert into tokenized form.   The first real transactions have already happened. On July 15, DTCC reported production trades involving more than 30 firms. The activity included collateral pledges, securities lending, Treasury financing and equity transactions. Assets were converted using DTCC's private Besu network and the Canton Network.   October is the planned broader service launch following that limited production activity. The distinction matters: a successful day of transactions establishes that a process can work. A continuing service must demonstrate that it can work reliably as more firms adopt it.  The mechanics begin with securities already held at DTC. When a participant requests tokenization, DTC moves the corresponding position into a dedicated account on its existing ledger and issues a token to a registered wallet. That token represents the participant's security entitlement. To return to conventional book-entry form, DTC destroys the token and credits the securities back to the participant's account.  DTCC says the tokenized form preserves the rights and investor protections of the traditional holding. The underlying securities remain registered in the name of DTC's nominee, Cede and Company. Investors continue to rely on the established custody framework.  In December 2025, @SECGov staff issued a conditional no-action letter covering the service for three years after the preliminary version launches. The SEC describes a voluntary pilot with operational limits, meaning a commercial launch can proceed within a limited regulatory framework.  The business case centers on making assets easier to use. Consider a firm holding Treasury securities while needing to post collateral elsewhere. If it can transfer an eligible tokenized position efficiently, and the receiving institution accepts it, the firm may be able to meet that obligation with fewer operational steps. Across large portfolios, even modest improvements could reduce costs and make existing holdings more useful.  DTCC points to collateral mobility and capital efficiency as potential benefits. The practical question is how much improvement survives the demands of real operations: compliance checks, funding arrangements, system integration and the willingness of counterparties to accept the assets.  There are boundaries. Under the initial no-action framework, tokenized entitlements receive no collateral or settlement value within DTC's own risk-management calculations. Firms can explore collateral uses outside those calculations, but tokenization does not automatically expand their capacity inside DTC.   DTCC also describes transfers between registered participant wallets on approved networks operating around the clock. That capability alone cannot make every stock market, broker or cash-payment system available twenty-four hours a day. Completing a purchase still requires arrangements for both the security and the money.   Controls remain central to the design. Transfers are restricted to registered wallets, and DTCC's token controls include freezing assets and reversing transfers when necessary. For institutions, the appeal is the ability to use blockchain while retaining mechanisms for compliance and recovery.   The network strategy is also broader than a single blockchain. July's transactions used Besu and Canton. DTCC has separately announced a connection with @StellarOrg, with DTC-tokenized assets expected there in the first half of 2027. That is a later milestone on the published timetable.  @Ripple Prime appears in DTCC's industry working group, too. That participation does not establish ripple:native as the service's settlement asset. Institutional involvement and demand for a particular cryptocurrency are separate questions, and investors should look for evidence connecting them.  As October approaches, the useful measures will be operational: whether the service launches on schedule, which firms use it repeatedly, how much value remains in tokenized form, and whether transfers produce measurable savings. Announced capacity matters less than sustained use.  For most individual investors, the first changes may occur behind the brokerage screen. Over time, successful adoption could influence the services their brokers offer and the cost of delivering them. Those outcomes will depend on execution and competition.  October gives Wall Street a chance to turn a demonstrated capability into a working business service. Its significance will become clearer in the months that follow, as firms decide whether tokenized securities are useful enough to become routine.  Reporting notes and sources Source 1. Stablecoins are tiny relative to the scale of US debt rollover and new deficit financing.  Yes, stablecoin growth creates incremental demand for short-dated US Treasuries.  But don’t confuse that with solving the Treasury’s funding problem.  Stablecoin reserves redirect existing private-sector dollars into T-bills. They can participate in demand for newly issued debt, but they don’t magically create the trillions in new savings required to absorb persistent deficits and refinancing.  That is not QE.  Primary dealers are required to participate in Treasury auctions, but they’re not the only buyers. Funds, banks, pensions, insurers and foreign institutions can absorb new issuance too. One thing I underestimated for years is how powerful a sustainable 5-7% APR return can be for long-term wealth, especially once your portfolio becomes large enough that protecting and compounding it matters almost as much as growing it.  That sent me back into portfolio management recently, and the part I find most interesting is where TradFi and DeFi now overlap: the “safe yield” bucket.  Traditionally, this is where you'd look at T-bills, money market funds or short-duration fixed income. But being crypto-native gives us another universe to compare against:  DeFi money markets.  My mental model here has changed quite a lot. Instead of constantly asking, “Where can I get the highest APY?”, I’m increasingly asking: “What is the smallest additional risk I need to take above cash or t-bills to earn a few extra percent?”  If I can consistently find 5-7% without taking stupid risk, that is already extremely powerful over a long enough time horizon. And once you start thinking this way, choosing where to deploy capital in DeFi starts looking much less like yield farming and much more like credit analysis.  Where does the yield actually come from? What collateral is backing the loans? Which stablecoin am I holding? What smart-contract, liquidity and oracle risks am I taking? And most importantly, am I actually being compensated enough for taking those risks?  A 6% yield looks boring in DeFi, especially when we're conditioned to look for things that can 10x. But you don't need every part of your portfolio to generate asymmetric upside.  You need some parts to simply survive, generate cash flow and compound for a very long time.  And I think this is one of the underrated advantages of being crypto-native today. We don't necessarily have to choose between TradFi and DeFi; we can put both on the same yield curve and compare what we're actually being paid for each additional layer of risk.  If T-bills give me X and a battle-tested DeFi money market gives me X+2%, the question isn't simply whether 2% more is attractive. The real question is whether that extra 2% adequately compensates me for stablecoin risk, smart-contract risk, collateral risk and liquidity risk.  The goal isn't to automatically move toward the highest number anymore.  It's to understand exactly where the yield comes from, what can go wrong, and whether I'm being paid enough for it.  That shift from chasing yield to pricing risk is probably the most interesting thing I've learned from going back to portfolio management.

I mapped the major asset-issuer combinations across the RWA market.  After removing the duplicated $1.46B reported under both Centrifuge and Janus Henderson, the issuers in this dataset represent roughly $19.9B in tokenized assets.  The market is much more concentrated than the number of available products suggests.  4 asset families currently account for almost everything.  [1] Treasuries, T-bills, and money market funds: ~$9.8B  This is still the largest RWA category, representing around 49% of the mapped value.  The main issuers are:  – @Hashnote_Labs: $2.98B – @BlackRock: $2.73B – @Ondo treasury products: $1.48B – Janus Henderson/@centrifuge JTRSY: $786M – @Spiko_finance: $783M – @SuperstateInc: $775M – @FTDA_US: $222M – @OpenEden_X: $21M  I think the attraction is straightforward.  These products give onchain investors access to short-duration government debt, dollar yield, and institutional fund structures without leaving crypto rails.  Spiko is especially interesting because it is the only issuer in this group with meaningful euro-denominated exposure.  EUTBL alone has reached approximately $452M.  [2] Gold: ~$5B  Tokenized gold represents around 25% of the mapped market, but the category is effectively a duopoly:  – Tether XAUT: $3.07B – Paxos PAXG: $1.90B  Both are single products deployed on Ethereum.  I find this significant because tokenized gold already has real scale, yet no third issuer has built a comparable position.  The product is simple, globally understood, and closely aligned with the macro demand for assets outside the traditional banking system.  [3] Equities and ETFs: ~$3.6B  This is the broadest category by product count, but its capital remains highly concentrated.  – @Ondo: around $2.27B in tokenized stocks and $660M in ETFs – @BackedFi: $610M across 68 products – @RobinhoodCrypto: $24M across 1,456 priced tokens – @DinariGlobal, Remora, and Swarm make up the remaining long tail  Ondo is currently the clear leader in both value and product coverage.  Robinhood shows the opposite model.  It offers the largest number of assets, including equities, ETFs, commodities, and private companies, but its average priced value is only around $17K per token.  That does not make the model unimportant. It shows that distribution can develop much faster than liquidity.  Robinhood is building the product surface first. The next test is whether capital, secondary-market liquidity, and DeFi utility follow.  [4] Structured credit and multi-asset funds: ~$1.5B  This remains a small and concentrated segment.  JAAA, the Janus Henderson AAA CLO fund, accounts for approximately $669M and is the only structured-credit product with meaningful scale in this dataset.  WisdomTree adds another $809M across 15 multi-asset fund share classes.  I see this category as strategically important because it expands tokenization beyond cash-equivalent assets.  However, its current depth is still limited compared with treasuries and gold.  The strongest pattern from this map is the inverse relationship between product breadth and capital depth.  Tether, Hashnote, BlackRock, and Paxos each operate one major product, yet together they hold more than $10B.  Robinhood offers 1,456 priced tokens but holds only $24M across them.  Capital is currently rewarding a small number of simple, liquid, easily understood assets.  A large product catalogue alone does not create demand.  The second pattern is distribution across chains.  XAUT, PAXG, and USTB are concentrated on Ethereum.  BUIDL spans seven chains, while Ondo’s equity products typically operate across three or four.  I think this will become a more important competitive variable.  Single-chain deployment can concentrate liquidity, but multichain distribution gives issuers access to more wallets, exchanges, collateral markets, and settlement environments.  My main conclusion is that the RWA market is developing through 2 different models:  → Capital concentration: a few products absorb billions because the underlying asset already has clear demand.  → Asset distribution: issuers tokenize hundreds or thousands of products first, then work to build liquidity and utility around them.  Right now, ~74% of the mapped value is still held in treasuries and gold.  The product universe is expanding quickly, but capital remains conservative.  The next stage will not be measured only by how many assets become tokenized.

Do You Really Need an iPhone 18?  The iPhone in this photo is ten years old. I just compared this iPhone 7 with its most recent sibling, and aside from aesthetics, there isn't much of a quantum leap between the two. The main differences are screen size and camera placement. The iPhone 18 obviously records better video, but with apps, you can improve the quality of shots you take on an iPhone 7, too.   In my opinion, most people don't need an iPhone 18. You may want it. But you don't need it. Your current iPhone can do almost everything the iPhone 18 will do. Your existing Samsung device can do most of what the iPhone 18 can. Even more interestingly, the iPhone can't do some of the feats your Samsung can. Yet, the iPhone 18 is an amazingly good phone.   Whether you buy one or not, in about a year, Apple will launch a new iPhone, and the iPhone 18 will become passé and lose up to 50% of its value. Or more.  Understand that the dictionary meaning of what an asset is is literally different from the accounting definition of the word asset.   According to the Oxford English Dictionary, an asset is anything that has value. But in strict accounting terms, an asset has present value and is expected to continue to have future financial value, especially one that increases or at least remains constant.   I leave it to you to decide, based on the definitions above (which you can fact-check), whether an iPhone 18 is an asset you need.   If you have $1299 or ₦2.5 million, you can multiply those funds by as much as 1000% in five years or less by investing in the Dangote Refinery IPO, which is likely to be oversubscribed.   Put in an average mutual fund, that money will definitely yield you at least $250. I know this because I have been benefiting from such funds for years, and apart from the #COVID19 downturn, mutual funds ALWAYS yield a handsome profit.   $60,000 in a mutual fund will give you about the same income as $360,000 in a fixed deposit. I am speaking from experience.   You can also multiply your wealth through ETFs, CDs, REITs, Treasury bills, Treasury bonds, lending clubs, crypto, and spot trading, with the last two being riskier and the others carrying very little peril.   Therefore, think twice before being carried away by consumerist trends. Remember, you have a life to live, and before feeding your ego, you may want to ensure you and your family are fed now and in the future.   But if you are making a fortune from social media posts, reels, and other audiovisual content, and an iPhone 18 will scale up your income, then by all means go for it. In your specific case, the iPhone 18 is likely an asset rather than a liability.   Bemigho Reno Omokri

The interesting thing about digital credit is that it does not need to replace traditional fixed income to become enormous.  It just needs to make the portfolio math better, and humans following rational incentives will do the rest.  At a 13% SATA yield versus 4% T-bills, every 5% of the portfolio moved from bills into SATA adds roughly 45 bps of annual income.  5% SATA: +45 bps. 10%: +90 bps. 20%: +180 bps.  At roughly 33% SATA / 67% bills, the portfolio yields about 7%.  That is a very different proposition from telling a fixed-income allocator to abandon the bond market and become a Bitcoiner.  You can leave most of the book in highly liquid, short-duration government paper and use digital credit as a smaller income engine.  And that is where I think the adoption story gets interesting.  Maybe the first allocators will be 1%. Then 3%. Then 5%.  But once the asset has a track record, the question changes.  Why are we extending duration across the portfolio, or taking worse credit risk elsewhere, when a relatively small SATA sleeve can move the portfolio yield this much? Nobody has to change their worldview for that trade to happen. The incentive is sitting right there in the math.  Digital credit can win a few percentage points of the portfolio at a time.  And a few percentage points of the global fixed-income market is an absurd amount of capital.

If you are looking to park cash for the short term, Treasury Bills (T-Bills) are a good alternative to bank fixed deposits.  On shorter tenures (91 and 182 days), T-Bills typically offer higher yields than matching bank FDs.  You can invest in T-Bills directly on Kite under Bids > Govt. Securities. The bidding window is open every week on Monday and Tuesday.  Here is a quick breakdown of how T-Bills work:  T-Bills are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India.  Unlike bonds, which pay periodic interest, T-Bills are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value (₹100) on maturity. The difference is your return.  For example, if you buy a T-Bill at a discounted price of ₹98, you receive the full ₹100 at maturity. The ₹2 difference is what you earn.  If you trade in the markets, you can also pledge 182-day and 364-day T-Bills for collateral margin and are considered cash-equivalent.

Stocks vs. MMFs, T-Bills and High-Yield Investment Schemes:  Stocks give you ownership in a company. When the company does well, the value of your investment can increase.  Some companies also pay dividends, providing an additional source of income.  The main advantage of investing in stocks is the potential for significant long-term growth.  If you invest in good companies and give your investment enough time, stocks can offer attractive returns and help you build wealth.  However, stocks come with higher risk and price fluctuations. Your investment can rise today and fall tomorrow. There is no guaranteed return, and if a company performs badly, you could lose part or almost all of your investment.  Money Market Funds (MMFs) and Treasury Bills (T-Bills) are generally more focused on preserving capital and providing relatively predictable returns.  They can be useful when you don't want to expose your money to the ups and downs of the stock market.  High-Yield Investment Schemes (HYIS) may promise or target higher returns, but the level of risk depends heavily on the particular scheme and what it actually invests in.  A higher advertised return does not necessarily mean it is a better investment. It is important to understand how the scheme generates its returns and the risks involved.  The simple difference:  1. Stocks: Better suited to someone willing to accept fluctuations in exchange for the possibility of stronger long-term growth.  2. MMFs: Generally suitable for preserving money while earning a return.  3. T-Bills: Generally lower-risk investments with more predictable returns.  4. HYIS: Can offer attractive returns, but the risk varies greatly, so the specific investment needs to be carefully examined.  Ultimately, there is no investment that gives high returns without some level of risk. The best option depends on what you're investing for, when you'll need the money, and how much risk you're comfortable taking.  AJD.

How much money do you actually need to start earning DeFi yield in 2026?  The answer depends heavily on what you mean by earning yield.  You can enter some DeFi strategies with a small amount, but becoming an operator can require far more capital.  Here’s where Seasons Builder Node changes the equation:  1/ The entry comparison  Ethereum validator 32 ETH minimum, plus hardware and ongoing operation.  Solana validator significant hardware and operating requirements.  Liquid staking: accessible with much less capital, but you are staking through a protocol and receiving a liquid staking asset.  Lending pools: low capital barriers, but yield depends on borrowing demand and market conditions.  Seasons Builder Node: 1,000 $SEAS minimum.  That threshold was reduced from 10,000 $SEAS to 1,000 $SEAS with Node Software v2.  2/ The important part is the hidden cost.  A 1,000 $SEAS Builder Node does not mean you only need exactly 1,000 $SEAS to buy in.  Seasons applies a 10% transfer fee on eligible buys and sells.  So if you want approximately 1,000 $SEAS net after the fee, you need roughly 1,112 $SEAS before the fee.  That cost matters when comparing entry barriers.  3/ But entry size is only half the story.  Different systems distribute yield differently.  With pooled DeFi, your return can depend on the pool, liquidity, fees, utilization, token incentives and the size of your position.  Seasons separates Builder and Director node weighting.  Builders compete against Builders, while Directors compete against Directors.  So a whale entering the Director tier does not directly dilute a Builder’s share by competing for the same tier weight.  4/ What can a small holder actually do?  With $250, you can access some lending and liquid staking strategies, depending on the platform and transaction costs.  But you cannot run an Ethereum validator with $250.  You also cannot meet Seasons’ 1,000 $SEAS Builder threshold with $250.  That distinction is important: Low cost DeFi access ≠ low cost node operation.  5/ Where Seasons becomes interesting is the operator style entry.  The Builder Node starts at 1,000 $SEAS and requires no dedicated hardware, no uptime commitment and no staking contract.  The wallet itself functions as the node.  Builders receive yield in $SEAS, which can be claimed and held toward the 10,000 $SEAS Director threshold.  That creates a progression path rather than simply distributing another asset.  6/ The trade off is obvious.  Builder yield being paid in $SEAS means greater exposure to the native token.  That can help someone progressing toward Director status, but it is not the same as receiving a diversified external asset basket.  At 10,000 $SEAS, the Director tier provides the broader payout structure.  So the best option depends on the objective.  7/ Here’s my simple verdict:  For passive staking exposure liquid staking such as Jito or Marinade can make more sense.  For lending based yield platforms such as Kamino can be more appropriate.  For traditional, lower volatility savings T-bills or a high yield savings account have advantages DeFi cannot replicate.  For someone specifically looking for a wallet native node with a lower operator threshold. Seasons Builder is the more relevant comparison.  8/ The key question is not simply: What has the highest APY?  Ask instead:  - How much capital do I need? - What fees do I pay? - Where does the yield come from? - What asset am I paid in? - What happens when I want out? - And what risks am I taking?  9/ Seasons is not risk free.  The 10% transfer fee is a real cost. $SEAS price exposure is another.  And unlike a bank deposit, a crypto position does not provide the same protections or dollar stability as traditional savings.  That is exactly why the comparison matters.  10/ If your goal is specifically to start earning with a small operator style position, the 1,000 $SEAS @SeasonsDEFI Builder threshold is the number to investigate.

A few points for Democratic senators deciding how to vote on the CLARITY Act:  1. If you are angry about political meme coins, the answer cannot be to preserve the regulatory vacuum that allowed them to flourish.  Trump’s $TRUMP coin demonstrated the conflicts and opportunities for abuse created when politicians can issue speculative assets without clear rules. Hunter Biden launching $LAPTOP immediately before this vote and watching it collapse almost instantly shows that this is not a problem confined to one party.  $LAPTOP lost roughly 95–98% of its value shortly after launch. That is a preview of what continued inaction produces: more political tokens, more speculation, more questionable launches and more retail investors left holding the losses.  The CLARITY Act will not eliminate every bad token. No financial law eliminates every bad product. But it creates federal oversight, registration requirements, enforcement authority and market rules where today there remains dangerous ambiguity.   The latest draft also adds restrictions on federal elected officials issuing digital assets and gives state attorneys general an enforcement role.  If the ethics provisions remain insufficient, strengthen them. Do not use legitimate objections to Trump’s conduct as a reason to preserve the system that enabled it. You have had nearly 2 years to address this all.  2.  Tens of millions of Americans own crypto.  Even conservative surveys put the number in the tens of millions. These are voters, consumers and investors, not merely an industry lobby.  Democrats have had more than a year of negotiations to propose amendments, safeguards and stronger enforcement provisions. The latest draft reportedly incorporates 126 substantive changes requested by Democrats, including significant ethics concessions.  Make no mistake about the political consequence: many crypto holders will not interpret the bill’s defeat as Trump failing to keep a promise.   They will see Democrats blocking the only major piece of legislation capable of replacing regulatory ambiguity with consumer protections and doing so to protect incumbent banks and pursue a political fight with Trump.  That may feel like a short-term political victory in Washington. Outside Washington, it is becoming an argument that Democrats chose politics over protecting market participants.  9/10 Crypto holders agree.  3. The United States cannot lead the next generation of financial technology without writing the rules under which it can be built.  The EU already has MiCA. Hong Kong’s stablecoin licensing regime took effect in 2025. Singapore has strengthened its digital-token framework, and the United Kingdom is opening its authorization process for its new crypto regime.... Russia, Japan... These are just a few examples.  Those jurisdictions began later in several cases, yet they have moved from debate to implementation while Washington remains stuck.  Capital, developers and businesses do not wait indefinitely. They incorporate, hire and build wherever the rules are understandable. Every additional delay gives competing financial centers time to attract infrastructure, talent and investment that should be developed in the United States.  Leadership does not mean deregulation. It means establishing rigorous rules quickly enough that responsible businesses can build under them, and regulators can identify and prosecute those who do not.  4. The evidence does not support using deposit-flight fears to justify a blanket prohibition on stablecoin yield.  Stablecoin reserves do not simply disappear from the financial system. Much of the money is redirected into bank deposits, Treasury bills and other reserve assets. The composition and distribution of funding can change, so the risk should be studied and managed, but “every dollar leaving a bank account destroys a dollar of lending” is not a serious description of the mechanics.  The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated that eliminating stablecoin yield would increase aggregate bank lending by only $2.1 billion, approximately 0.02%, while imposing an estimated net welfare cost of $800 million by denying consumers competitive returns.  The case for an outright ban is far weaker than bank lobbyists suggest and most americans are mad that the banking interests and lobbying takes a precedent over them.   Use reserve requirements, disclosure rules, liquidity standards and appropriate limits to address genuine financial-stability risks. Do not suppress consumer competition merely to protect the cheapest source of funding enjoyed by incumbent banks.  All in all  Democratic senators face a legitimate choice: improve the legislation or preserve the vacuum.  But voting no does not punish Trump. It leaves consumers with fewer protections, entrenches regulatory uncertainty, protects incumbent interests and gives foreign jurisdictions more time to take America’s lead. Tokenization doesn’t magically make an RWA liquid  There’s a common misconception that putting a real-world asset onchain makes it behave like Bitcoin or a public stock.  It doesn’t.  Tokenization changes how an asset is recorded, transferred and used. It doesn’t automatically change the asset, the legal structure, or the number of buyers.  Here’s what that means:  1. A token doesn’t create a market  Putting a property, private fund or collectible onchain doesn’t guarantee someone will buy it.  Tokenization can make transfers, ownership records and settlement more efficient, but liquidity still depends on demand and distribution.  An illiquid asset can remain illiquid with a token attached to it.  2. You often own a claim, not the asset itself  Take BlackRock’s BUIDL.  You aren’t holding individual Treasury bills onchain.  You hold shares in a fund that owns cash, T-bills and other assets, with the ownership record represented through tokens.  The benefit is mainly operational:  faster settlement → easier transfers between eligible participants → programmable onchain use  The underlying assets and legal structure still matter.  3. Blockchain doesn’t remove credit risk  Tokenizing private credit doesn't make the borrower more likely to repay.  If the borrower defaults, the loan can still default.  If collateral isn't properly secured, a token doesn't magically fix that either.  Blockchain can improve things like transparency, settlement and record-keeping, but it doesn't replace underwriting, legal enforcement or collateral.  The better way to think about RWA tokenization:  Asset → legal structure → token → distribution → liquidity → onchain utility  Tokenization can improve several steps in that process.  But it doesn't magically fix the others.  The real innovation is making traditional financial assets easier to record, transfer, distribute and plug into onchain financial infrastructure.

The minimum capital requirement for a merchant bank is N50 billion, approximately $38 million.  The question is: Will this money remain with the CBN forever?  The answer is NO.  So, where will the money go?  Section 3(2) of the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020 requires the shareholders of a proposed bank to deposit the applicable minimum paid-up share capital with the CBN after submitting the required documentation.  But what happens next?  Scenario 1: The licence is approved.  Under Section 4(2)(b) of BOFIA 2020, the CBN is required to repay the deposited capital, together with the investment income, to the licensed institution. The investment income is treated as income of the institution.  The bank can then deploy its capital into permissible banking activities, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.  Scenario 2: The licence is not approved.  Section 4(2)(a) provides that the CBN shall repay the deposited capital to the applicant, together with the investment income, after deducting administrative expenses and tax on the income.  In other words, the law provides for the return of the capital in both scenarios.  The CBN may invest the deposited funds in Treasury bills or other permitted securities while it considers the application, as provided under Section 4(1).  The takeaway?  The N50 billion is not intended to remain idle with the CBN forever. It serves as evidence of the required capital during the licensing process and, once the licence is granted, is returned to the licensed institution for its banking business.

The S&P 500 has compounded at roughly 10 percent a year long term with dividends reinvested. Ten thousand dollars invested in 1996 would have grown to about 192 thousand dollars by the end of 2025. Over longer windows the numbers get even more extreme because of compounding.⁠  Most people never capture that return. DALBAR’s studies show the average equity investor trails the market by 1 to 3 percent or more per year simply from behavior: selling during crashes, buying near tops, and overtrading. The longer the horizon, the more devastating the difference.⁠  There is one important caveat. Randomly buying individual stocks and holding forever usually does not work. Hendrik Bessembinder’s research on a century of U.S. stocks found the median stock returned negative 6.9 percent, and nearly 60 percent of stocks lost money relative to Treasury bills. A tiny fraction of companies created almost all the wealth. Quality with durable competitive advantages or broad diversification that captures the winners is what actually works.⁠  Warren Buffett’s famous line is that his favorite holding period is forever, but he means for outstanding businesses, not for every stock he buys. A bank's reserve report is already a public document. The failure point is the gap between the PDF and the accounts that supposedly back it.  An auditor samples. A regulator receives a snapshot. A counterparty receives a letter. None of those parties re-runs the TLS session against the custodian, the bank, or the chain at the moment the claim is made. The number can be true on Tuesday and untrue on Thursday, and every recipient of the report is still holding Tuesday.  That is the part of institutional onchain finance that public ledgers do not fix. A public ledger can show a token balance. It cannot show that the offchain cash, T-bills, or broker account behind that token still matches, unless someone re-fetches the source and proves the fetch. Publishing the fetch publishes the account.  @primus_labs splits those two jobs. zkTLS lets an attestor prove an HTTPS response came from the real server, without the attestor reading the raw session. FHE then lets the encrypted figures be summed, compared, and checked against a threshold, with only the authorized party able to decrypt. The output a counterparty needs is a pass or a shortfall. The output they do not need is the position book.  This is already in production use, not a roadmap slide. A Fed cut cycle is the textbook catalyst for a bull steepener, and that is exactly what pulls US commercial banks into T-bills.  ⭕️The view: the gap between short and long yields widens. The execution: buy the short end (T-bills or the 2-year) and short the long end (the 10-year or 30-year). On macro desks that is called a bull steepener.  Why a cut widens the spread: the 2-year is anchored to policy. When the Fed cuts, short yields reprice down immediately as funding costs fall. The long end is driven by growth, inflation expectations, and the term premium from deficits. It falls slower, or stays elevated if the market thinks easier policy revives inflation later. Short yields drop faster than long yields, so the spread widens (or in the imminent future long yields might rise regardless).  🔶That is the bank’s natural trade.  Commercial banks borrow short (deposits, repo) and lend or invest long (mortgages, corporate loans, duration). Net interest margin is the spread. A steeper curve widens NIM. A flat or inverted curve crushes it. The balance sheet is structurally long the widener. Desks lean in for the same reason, plus carry. In an upward curve, long the 2-year and short the 10-year earns positive carry if the curve does not move: you are paid the higher short-leg yield against cheaper funding, while the short long-bond hedges outright rate risk.  🎯So the Fed does not have to order banks to buy bills. Cut the funds rate, the front end collapses, the curve steepens, carry turns positive, and NIM math does the rest. Banks buy T-bills because that is the long leg of the only duration spread trade their balance sheet is built to want.

Treasuries: The Fed’s costly growth reflex  The Federal Reserve is part of America’s fiscal problem. It should be part of the solution, not by financing deficits, but by recognising that stronger growth need not mean higher inflation.  The data offer grounds for that distinction: trimmed-mean PCE inflation at 2 %, food-at-home CPI inflation at 2.1 %, below its long-term average, rising productivity and solid employment.   These look like the green shoots of Trump’s supply-side agenda: growth supported by expanding capacity rather than simply stronger demand. Rate-sensitive sectors are hurting. AI infrastructure and reshoring investment tell a different story.   Treating these divergent forces as one overheating economy mistakes productive investment for excessive demand.  The fiscal consequences are substantial. Federal interest costs now exceed spending on either defence or Medicare. Marketable Treasury debt carries an average rate around 3.4%, while maturing coupon debt faces refinancing rates roughly 1.4 percentage points higher. Nearly $7 T of Treasury bills mature within a year. Another 75-basis-point Fed increase would add approximately $50 B to their annual interest cost alone.  The danger is circular. Higher rates widen deficits, requiring more borrowing. Greater long-dated issuance can lift term premiums, raising borrowing costs again. Interest payments absorb resources without expanding productive capacity, potentially crowding out investment.  The Fed cannot repair Washington’s budget. Treasury management: Ripple Treasury (formerly GTreasury, acquired for approximately $1 billion)—a software platform used by over a thousand corporations to manage their cash, including American Airlines, Subway, and—as of today—Robinhood.  Distribution: Robinhood, with its 28.6 million clients, integrating RLUSD into its app; and DriveWealth, which serves over 100 brokerage firms. No bank in the world possesses all eight layers. JPMorgan has five; BNY has two; Visa has one and a half. Ripple is bringing them ALL together.  And do you know where the real business lies? A stablecoin can be fully backed and still fail to give you your $1 back.  Reserves are only the first layer. Whether $1 actually stays $1 also depends on who can redeem, where the reserves sit, who controls the contract and which chain you're on.  There are seven layers in total. I went through each one, using USDC and USDT as examples.  ---  ► 1. Reserves  This is what backs the supply. For a fiat-backed stablecoin it's usually:  - US Treasury bills - Treasury repos - Cash and bank deposits - Government money market funds  $USDC as of November 23, 2026:  - Circulation: $67.9B - Reserves: $68.2B - Coverage: ~100.4%  About 86.5% of that sits in T-bills and repos. Still, safe assets aren't the same as instant cash. Maturities, settlement times and access to banks all matter when everyone wants out at once.  ---  ► 2. Legal claim  Holding a stablecoin doesn't mean you can cash it in with the issuer.  USDC: - Only eligible, registered @circle customers can redeem directly - Access depends on account eligibility, compliance and local rules  USDT: - Direct redemption needs verification and approval - Minimum redemption: $100,000 - Fee: $1,000 or 0.1%, whichever is higher - Verification fee: $150, non-refundable  So there are really two markets. Big, verified players redeem with the issuer. Everyone else exits through exchanges, brokers, OTC desks or DeFi pools, and relies on those players to keep the price at $1.  ---  ► 3. Compliance  Before paying anyone out, the issuer has to know who they are and whether the transaction is allowed. That means:  - KYC and KYB - AML and sanctions screening - Transaction monitoring - Source-of-funds checks  None of this is visible onchain, and any of it can slow down or block a redemption, even when the reserves are all there.  ---  ► 4. Custody  It also matters where the reserves are actually held.  For USDC, most of the reserve sits in the Circle Reserve Fund (USDXX), managed by @BlackRock and held at BNY Mellon. The rest is cash at regulated banks.  The risks here are less about the assets and more about the institutions: bank exposure, a custodian failing, or settlement getting stuck. USDC learned this the hard way in 2023, when part of its reserves got caught in the SVB collapse.  ---  ► 5. Mint and burn  This is where offchain dollars turn into onchain tokens.  To mint, an eligible customer sends USD, the issuer confirms it and sends new tokens to their wallet. To redeem, the customer sends tokens back, the issuer burns them and wires the dollars.  Circle publishes these flows every week. In the 30 days to November 23, it minted $54.8B of USDC and burned $57.3B, so supply shrank by $2.5B.  ---  ► 6. Smart contracts  The contract decides what the token can do, and what the issuer can still do to it.  - `mint` and `burn`: create and destroy tokens - `pause`: stop transfers - `blacklist`: block addresses - `freeze`: lock balances - `admin/owner`: control all of the above  This is the trade-off people often forget. The same controls that make a stablecoin compliant also mean the issuer can stop your tokens from moving.  ---  ► 7. Blockchain  The same stablecoin can behave very differently depending on where it lives.  Things to check: - Native vs wrapped versions - The right contract address - Bridges and cross-chain messaging - Fees and finality  USDC uses CCTP to move natively between chains. It burns USDC on one chain, Circle signs an attestation, and the same amount is minted on the other.  Bridged USDC is a different story. It carries the bridge's risk on top of Circle's, and liquidity can be thin on some networks.  ---  Reserves get most of the attention, but they're one layer out of seven. The real question is how all of them hold up when a lot of people want out at the same time.
