You own a house worth ₦180 million, a car worth ₦25 million and have an emergency reserve of ₦15 million. That leaves ₦219 million in investable capital.  A diversified portfolio comprising Treasury bills, FGN bonds, money market funds, Eurobonds and global equities, split equally between naira and foreign-currency assets, could generate approximately ₦20.3 million in annual investment income, or ₦1.69 million monthly, under reasonable assumptions.  However, you cannot sustainably spend your entire nominal return. If your investment generates a net return of 15.67% and inflation is 14.06%, your real return is only 1.41%. Spending the entire nominal return erodes the purchasing power of your capital. And this is me just being generous with the 14% inflation because we all know whatsup.  Now, consider a reasonable monthly retirement budget: ₦400k for food, ₦250k for utilities, ₦200k for transportation, ₦200k for home maintenance, ₦150k for domestic assistance, ₦150k for personal expenses, ₦100k for family obligations and ₦250k for healthcare. Add an annual international travel budget of $4,000, and you're spending approximately ₦25.8 million annually, or ₦2.15 million monthly.  Btw, when i say reasonable, I mean you'll actually be struggling a bit, and i assume you have no debt and have no dependent children or plan to be dependent on them.  Healthcare expenses also increase as you age. Your medical needs at 65 will be different from when you're 85. I've assumed an additional ₦6 million annually for elderly care from age 85 and ₦20 million for a major medical emergency, both in today's money.  Then there's currency depreciation. Assuming 10% annual naira depreciation and 3% foreign inflation, that $4,000 travel budget, which costs ₦5.4 million today, would cost ₦18.9 million in ten years and ₦65.9 million in twenty years. If you build a model that incorporates 12% domestic inflation, 15% healthcare inflation, 10% currency depreciation, investment returns net of estimated taxes and fees, periodic vehicle replacement, medical emergencies and elderly care, the ₦219 million investment portfolio would be exhausted around age 74.  Even if the entire $324,000 were investable, with housing provided separately, the portfolio would become insufficient around age 83.  Personally, I would consider $850,000–$1 million in net worth. Something BIG is happening in Nigeria’s banking sector, and I don’t think most Nigerians are paying attention.  The CBN is changing the rules of how money moves, how banks operate, how fintech companies function and even how much it costs you to borrow or save money.  But what does all this really mean for the ordinary Nigerian?  Your Savings and Loans  The CBN has reduced interest rates. In simple English, borrowing money could gradually become cheaper. But there is another side to it. The attractive interest rates banks offer on fixed deposits and Treasury bills may also begin to drop.  If you have money sitting somewhere earning high interest, pay attention. Those returns may not last forever.  Your Fintech Apps Are Coming Under the Radar  That money in your OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay and other fintech accounts is becoming part of a much tighter regulatory environment.  The government wants greater control and oversight of major financial technology companies.  Think about it this for a sec, the platforms Nigerians increasingly depend on to receive, transfer and store money are becoming too important to operate without serious regulatory supervision.  This could mean better protection, but also more monitoring, stricter verification and fewer opportunities to operate outside the conventional banking system.  Banks Are Raising Trillions. Why?  Nigerian banks have been raising billions and trillions of naira to strengthen their financial positions.  On the surface, this is about protecting depositors and making banks stronger.  But think deeper. A stronger banking system also means greater capacity to control credit, finance businesses, influence economic activities and expand digital financial services.  The institutions holding your money are preparing for a different financial landscape.  The Naira and Dollar  Nigeria’s foreign reserves have reportedly crossed $55 billion. If this improvement is sustained, it could mean less pressure on the naira and more predictable foreign exchange transactions.  For businesses importing goods, parents paying foreign tuition and people making international payments, this matters.  But don’t celebrate too early. A stronger reserve position does not automatically mean a permanently stronger naira.  Now, here is what I find interesting.  Look at the bigger picture.  Interest rates are changing. Banks are recapitalising. Fintech companies are facing tighter regulation. Foreign exchange policies are evolving.  At the same time, more Nigerians are moving their money away from physical cash and into digital financial platforms.  Do you think it’s a Coincidence? Perhaps.  But one thing is clear: the structure of Nigeria’s financial system is changing, and the government wants a much stronger regulatory grip over the institutions through which money flows.  This is not necessarily a bad thing. A properly regulated financial system can protect people.  However, the more dependent we become on digital financial institutions, the more important it becomes to understand who regulates them, who controls the infrastructure and what happens when access to your money is restricted.

The people who owned those same funds made 8.7%, because they bought and sold at the wrong times. In the most volatile funds the gap was 2.1% a year. In the calmest ones, 0.4%. Even index fund investors lost 1.1% a year doing this.  JPMorgan: 20 years in the S&P got you 11.3% a year. Miss the 10 best days and that gets cut by more than half. And 6 of the 10 best days came within 2 weeks of the 10 worst. The guy who panic sold the crash missed the bounce.  The people who won:  1. They sat through drops that make most people quit. Bessembinder took the top 100 wealth creators of each decade. Even in their best decade, the average one fell 32.5% at some point. In the decade before, 51.6%. Netflix fell almost 80% during the 2010s, the best decade it ever had.  2. They owned companies that were actually growing. RWA yields ranked: tokenized T-bills, stocks, credit. Which one is worth it?  Would you take 4.8% in private credit over 3.7% in tokenized T-bills? Because that extra 1.1% is only ~$110/year on $10K.  Now ask yourself what risks you're taking for those $110.  1/ Tokenized T-bills  – 3M US Treasuries yield around 4%, while most tokenized Treasury products are paying 3.2–3.8% net.  – USDY has $2.4B AUM at 3.68%.  – BUIDL has $2.08B at 3.75%.  Nothing crazy. But the yield comes from actual government debt, not token emissions.  Over 30D, BENJI grew ~11%, USDY +5.1%, while BUIDL fell 7.6% and USTB dropped 21.4%.  So distribution, liquidity, redemption mechanics and DeFi utility are starting to matter more.  The real unlock imo is making that 3.7% yield-bearing asset usable as collateral, so capital doesn't have to just sit idle.  2/ Tokenized equities  $10B+ monthly trading volume against ~$3.6B in tokenized value is pretty wild.  Clearly there's demand for trading stocks onchain. But a tokenized stock doesn't magically generate yield just because it's onchain.  Outside dividends, we're relying on lending fees, LP fees, options premiums or incentives.  – @DinariGlobal's dShares can pass through dividends, roughly 1–2% on broad equity exposure depending on the asset.  – @xStocksFi lending vaults offer around 2%.  – Some @Raydium xStock LP pools show 5–10%+ APY.  but LPs are market-making volatile equities, taking inventory risk, adverse selection and potential IL, while hoping volume stays high enough to pay them.  if tokenized equity volume keeps ripping, efficient LPs could print from real fees. But once liquidity crowds in or incentives dry up, those APYs can get nuked pretty fast.  so i'm bullish on tokenized equities as a market structure play, not blindly bullish on their displayed yields.  3/ Private credit  Why earn 3.7% on Treasuries when private credit offers 7 -10%?  Well, because that spread is compensation for taking risk, not a gift. and the headline borrower rate is not necessarily what depositors earn.  @maplefinance has $4.82B in managed assets and $2.92B TVL, with syrupUSDC at ~4.8% and syrupUSDT at ~4.3%.  Borrowers may pay 6 -10%, but that isn't what depositors take home.  syrupUSDC at 4.8% vs USDY at 3.68% is only 112 bps extra.  for that premium, we're adding borrower risk, collateral risk, liquidation execution risk, smart contract risk and potentially slower exits.  Suddenly the higher APY doesn't look so sexy.  Same thing with an 8% credit pool.  If credit losses eat 3 percentage points, we're effectively left with ~5% before other costs.  We're taking a whole different risk profile to beat Treasuries by 130 bps. One bad default can wipe out years of that spread.  Doesn't mean credit is a bad trade. I actually like transparent, short-duration, well-collateralized lending.  So where's the best place to deploy capital?  For sustainable, risk-adjusted yield, my ranking is: T-bills > selective private credit > tokenized equity yield farms.  But for upside, i'd almost flip the ranking.  Tokenized equities have the bigger growth optionality, especially if trading volume keeps scaling and organic fees become meaningful.  Credit has room for selective opportunities, while Treasuries remain the base layer for capital.  DYOR.

Game Theory : What would be the best way for the fed and treasury, the mag 10 companies and the government to adopt stablecoin as money and bitcoin as a reserve asset?  People - note how this is literally playing out in front of our eyes.   The most workable path is sequenced: make stablecoins legally equivalent to dollars first, keep bitcoin on Treasury's balance sheet rather than the Fed's, and have big tech distribute rather than issue. This is how advocates would design it, not settled policy, and several pieces would need Congress.  1. Fed and Treasury: make stablecoins "real" dollars - Finish the rulebook: one-to-one backing, redemption at par, and clear priority for holders if an issuer fails. Treasury's August proposal targets January 18, 2027 as the framework's start date. - Settle in central bank money. A payment-only account floated by the Fed in May would let eligible firms clear and settle directly, short of a full master account. - Accept stablecoins for taxes and federal payments. Under MMT, tax acceptance is what makes something money, so this step matters more than any legal-tender label.       - Decide the backstop up front. Without Fed liquidity in a run, it isn't money; with it, issuers are effectively banks. 2. Bitcoin: reserve asset, never backing - Hold it at Treasury, like gold. A central bank buying an asset that competes with its own liabilities sends the wrong signal.      - Put it in statute. The current reserve rests on a March 2025 executive order that keeps forfeited bitcoin and bars selling it, and a former White House adviser says buying on the open market requires Congress to authorize it. - Fund it without new debt (forfeitures, or ARMA's idea of revaluing gold certificates to market price), on a pre-announced schedule, with audited custody.       - Never promise convertibility. A dollar pegged to bitcoin would end the elastic money MMT depends on.  3. Mag 10: rails, not mints - Build interoperable wallets into phones, stores and cloud, on open standards, so no single firm owns the money. - Accept stablecoins for checkout, payroll and supplier payments, and hold corporate cash in tokenized T-bills. - Stay out of issuance. Keeping commerce and banking separate is what makes this politically survivable.  4. Government: keep the exits open Preserve cash, bank deposits and self-custody as legal options. Adoption by choice is durable; adoption by lock-in invites the backlash your diagram describes.  Main objections - Deposits leaving banks could shrink lending. - Leaning on short-term bills raises rollover risk. - Bitcoin's volatility puts taxpayers on the hook, and Democratic critics led by Maxine Waters contend a bitcoin reserve would weaken the dollar's reserve-currency standing. ARMA cleared its House committee on a 28-21 party-line vote, so it's far from consensus.

H1 2026 showed how fragmented institutional crypto demand really was, with different pools of capital seeking different exposures.  Lumping ETFs, DATs, and onchain Treasuries together as institutional adoption glosses over what that capital is actually buying.  1/ ETFs gave crypto a distribution channel. The ETH data shows how easily that channel can run in reverse.  Spot ETH ETF holdings fell from 6M+ ETH to 5.2M during the first half.  An accessible investment wrapper makes it easier to enter a position and easier to exit it. Its existence doesn’t make the underlying allocation permanent.  Also, ETF balances aren’t a clean measure of institutional ownership. They describe assets held through a product that serves different types of investors.  The ETH ETF complex was cutting exposure over this stretch. Institutions getting access didn’t mean demand would keep coming.  2/ DATs were taking the other side.  Digital asset treasury companies increased their ETH holdings from 6M to 7.7M over the same period, overtaking spot ETFs.  By the end of H1:  – Spot ETFs held 5.2M ETH. – DATs held 7.7M ETH. – Together, they held close to 11% of ETH supply.  That changes who matters at the margin. Corporate treasury decisions became a larger part of ETH’s ownership structure, with @BitMNR a major driver of the accumulation.  But these figures don’t establish that ETF sellers directly funded DAT purchases. They show two ownership channels moving in opposite directions.  I separate DAT demand from Ethereum activity. Building a corporate ETH treasury adds demand for ETH, but there’s no automatic link to more borrowing, trading, or fees on the network.  ETH fell 47% during H1 even as DAT holdings grew. A growing buyer base can absorb supply without overpowering the rest of the market.  3/ Onchain Treasuries represent a different allocation altogether. The Financial System Is Being Rebuilt in Front of Us  Oil, inflation, the Fed, Treasury debt, gold, stablecoins, blockchain, Ripple, the SEC and $XRP are all hitting the same financial system from different angles. Once you follow the money between them, the connections get easier to see.  Higher oil prices feed inflation, and inflation keeps pressure on the Fed. Higher rates raise borrowing costs while making cash, Treasury bills and money market funds more attractive.  The U.S. has more than $40 trillion in debt and constantly needs buyers for Treasury securities. Stablecoins are becoming part of that system because regulated dollar tokens can hold short term Treasuries and other liquid assets in reserve.  Digital dollars can move on blockchain rails while the money underneath them is tied directly to banks, money markets and U.S. government debt. That connects crypto infrastructure directly back to traditional finance.  The current administration has pushed toward private digital money instead of a retail Federal Reserve CBDC. The GENIUS Act creates the federal framework for stablecoin reserves, redemptions, custody and supervision.  RLUSD fits inside that structure. Standard Custody issues it, BNY handles major custody responsibilities, and Ripple National Trust Bank adds federal supervision around reserve management and fiduciary custody.  The SEC environment changed too. Ripple’s case left a major distinction between $XRP itself and the way certain sales were conducted, with certain institutional sales violating securities law while programmatic sales were treated differently.  Traditional finance is moving onto digital rails at the same time. Money market funds are being represented on XRPL, DTCC is tokenizing securities entitlements, banks are adding digital asset custody and public ledgers are adding permissioned markets.  Now add digital dollars, tokenized bank deposits, euros, yen, Treasuries, securities, commodities and other stablecoins. Every new asset creates more markets and more separate pools of liquidity that eventually need to connect.  This is where $XRP can have a real job. XRPL can route value through $XRP when the direct market between two assets doesn’t have enough liquidity, while a better direct pair can settle without using it.  Take an oil transaction between a buyer in Japan and a producer in the Middle East. The buyer operates in yen, the oil may be priced in dollars, and the seller may ultimately want dollars or another currency.  Traditional correspondent banking can require capital to sit pre-funded across different countries and currencies. Digital rails can reduce some of that drag by moving through whatever liquidity route works best at the time.  Tokenized Treasuries could provide collateral, permissioned markets could control counterparties, stablecoins could handle the cash side, and $XRP could bridge liquidity when the direct market isn’t deep enough. None of that requires oil to be priced in $XRP or every transaction to touch it.  The use case is moving value between markets that would otherwise need separate pools of liquidity and pre-funded capital. As finance creates more digital forms of money, securities and commodities, connecting those pools becomes a bigger problem.  $XRP was built around moving value between different assets and different pools of liquidity. How large that role becomes will come down to liquidity, cost, regulation and whether institutions actually choose that route.

Earn first. Lose first.  That is not a warning buried in the docs. That is literally the deal with @realfi_co , and it is why I stopped scrolling.  Most protocols make you dig for who takes the loss. The yield is on the front page, the risk is somewhere in the small print. Here they split it into two tokens and write the order upfront. USDrf is the one you just hold, designed to track $1, keep it in your wallet and use it whenever. sUSDrf is the one you opt into. You stake USDrf and the return comes from real world lending, loans to real businesses, money market funds, that kind of boring stuff.  Holding and earning are two separate decisions here. If you only want the simple side, you stay in USDrf and earn nothing, because you are not taking that side of the deal. If you want the return, you consciously opt in, and opting in means accepting the other side too.  And when I say boring, I mean it in a good way. The portfolio behind it is not some mystery farm. It is Treasury bills and money market funds on the liquid side, CLO ETFs and direct lending on the other side, with the borrower's own equity sitting underneath the loans as a buffer. You can disagree with the mix, but at least you can see the mix. Their transparency portal shows the allocation and the reserves, so you are not just trusting a number on a dashboard.  That portal matters. Anyone can write "backed by real world assets" on a landing page, it costs nothing. Showing the allocation is different, because now I can ask how much is actually liquid, how much is in direct lending, and whether the mix changed. I might not like every answer, but at least I am judging something real.  In good times nobody cares about the loss order, because there is no loss to take. It only matters when something goes wrong, which is exactly when most people find out a product was never structured the way they imagined. Here it is not a surprise for later.  There is a catch, and honestly the catch made me trust it more, not less. Opting in is not instant in and out. The staked side has a cooldown, around seven days, because the money behind it is in things that cannot be sold in one click. That is the real trade. You want the return from real lending, you accept that your money moves at the speed of real lending, not at the speed of a swap button. It also filters itself: money you might need fast was probably never the right money to stake.  And the yield is variable, not promised. It moves with the portfolio, up or down, and nobody at RealFi is allowed to pretend otherwise. It is also not a bank deposit, so safe here is a relative word, not a guarantee.  It went live on Cardano mainnet on Oct 1, with Lace, Liqwid and SundaeSwap already plugged in, so it is not just sitting inside one app either. Most yield stories I see start on EVM chains. This one started on Cardano first, and that alone made me read it twice.  Question I am still asking myself: do you prefer your dollars completely idle and simple, or do you opt in when the risk order, the cooldown, and the portfolio are all this explicit?

How does Ottawa finance its federal debt? The old-fashioned way... it borrows.  Most of it is done by auctioning Treasury bills and Government of Canada bonds to banks, dealers, pension funds, and foreign investors.  Year after year the bulk of the new issuance just refinances debt that’s coming due. The rest covers the deficit. That’s the machine.  Use one credit card to pay off the interest on another.  The Bank of Canada is the government’s banker and auction agent.  In normal times it buys a modest slice of new issues (historically around 15-20% of bonds) to match its own balance sheet needs, mostly bank notes. It earns interest on those bonds and, after covering its costs, remits the profit back to Ottawa, usually around a billion a year.  That tiny portion of the debt is cheaper for taxpayers because the interest largely cycles back.  During COVID the Bank went big on quantitative easing and bought hundreds of billions. It also lost billions in the years after.    Today, the Bank of CAnada  still holds roughly 9% of outstanding Government of Canada securities. The rest is held by the private market.  Most of the $60+ billion that taxpayers pay in interest goes to private and foreign holders.  It's a real cost. It's money that can’t go to programs or tax cuts.   Interest paid on the slice that the Bank of CAnada holds is normally recycled.  But after the pandemic bond-buying binge, higher rates produced multi-year losses at the Bank (it pays more on the deposits it created than it earns on the old low-coupon bonds). Remittances stopped and those losses land on the government’s books....which falls on taxpayers because the BAnk of Canada is a Crown corporation. That’s an extra cost from the Quantitative Easing experiment.   The real cost is simpler: large ongoing deficits mean rising debt, rising interest costs (already tens of billions a year), and less room for everything else. The Bank of Canada doesn’t make the debt free.  It just manages the mechanics.

The reason your credit card charges you 22% is that back in 1980, Citibank wrote its own law and South Dakota passed it in a single day.  Citi was losing a fortune on credit cards back then. New York capped card interest at 12%, but inflation had pushed what Citi paid to borrow money up near 20%. Their chairman, Walter Wriston, later put it plainly. They were lending at 12 and paying 20, and you didn't have to be Einstein to see they were headed out of business. The card unit had already lost more than $1 billion.  New York wouldn't budge, so Citi's people called South Dakota's governor, Bill Janklow. Four times in one day.  South Dakota was broke. Farmers were paying almost 50 cents a bushel just to haul wheat that sold for $2.20, and the state was already working on getting rid of its interest rate cap. Citi offered 400 jobs if South Dakota would invite its card business in. According to Janklow, Citibank drafted the bill itself, and his legislature passed it in one day.  What made a South Dakota law matter to somebody in Ohio was a Supreme Court case from December 1978. A bank in Nebraska had been mailing credit cards to people in Minnesota at 18%, even though Minnesota capped rates at 12%. The Court sided with the bank unanimously. Whatever state your bank calls home gets to set your rate, no matter where you live.  Delaware passed its own version a year later, and the big New York banks packed up their card operations and moved there. Pretty much every credit card in America has been running on that one-day law for 46 years, which is why state rate caps have mostly been for show ever since.  A federal cap would be the first time the banks had nowhere to move.  Congress has come close before. In November 1991, President Bush mentioned at a fundraiser that he'd like to see card rates come down. The next day Senator Al D'Amato tacked a 14% cap onto a banking bill, and it passed the Senate 74 to 19 after about half an hour of debate. The Dow fell 120 points that Friday, the White House backed away, and the House let it die within days.  Back then the average card charged about 19% while Treasury bills paid 4.6%, so cards ran roughly 14 points above what the government paid to borrow. That was enough to get 74 senators to vote yes in an afternoon. Today the average card that charges interest sits at 22.36%, and the Fed's benchmark rate is under 4%. The spread is bigger now than it was the week the Senate lost its patience.  The politics are weirder this time too. Trump called for a 10% cap back in January. Josh Hawley and Bernie Sanders already have a 10% bill. And Elizabeth Warren is expected to run the Senate Banking Committee when Democrats take over Congress in January.  If something like this actually passes, keep an eye on the fees. In 1980, when Carter froze new credit card signups for a few months, the banks used the moment to start charging a $20 annual fee, and almost nobody canceled. The last time Washington squeezed card pricing, a brand new fee showed up within months.

The apparent paradox of Kenyan banks posting record super profits—such as KCB Group’s KSh 47.3 billion in Q3 2025 net profit and Equity Bank Kenya’s KSh 40.7 billion in Q3 2026—while the broader economy stagnates and loan defaults soar is not an accident, nor is it a sign of a thriving private sector. Instead, it is the logical outcome of how modern banking operates when high risk in the real economy meets lucrative, state-backed alternatives and concentrated market power.  ​When businesses struggle and household incomes shrink, commercial banks do not simply absorb the downturn alongside their customers; they pivot. With sector-wide gross non-performing loans hovering around KSh 696.9 billion—roughly 15% to 16% of the entire loan book—lenders sharply curtail credit to small businesses and everyday borrowers, effectively rationing out the very people who need capital most.   Rather than leaving customer deposits idle, banks channel billions of shillings into Kenyan Treasury bills and bonds. Because the government’s appetite for domestic borrowing remains high, these instruments offer double-digit, virtually risk-free returns, often enhanced by tax exemptions on infrastructure bonds. In practice, banks take cheap deposits from ordinary citizens and lend them to the state at high interest, locking in guaranteed profits while starving the private sector of affordable credit.  ​This dynamic is amplified by the wide, asymmetric gap between what banks pay savers and what they charge borrowers. A massive proportion of deposits in Tier-1 institutions sits in current and transactional accounts earning virtually zero interest, while savings accounts yield modest single-digit returns. On the other side of the ledger, under risk-based pricing frameworks approved by the Central Bank of Kenya, banks price commercial and personal loans steeply to buffer against default risk. Even when benchmark policy rates begin to fall, commercial lending rates remain notoriously slow to adjust downward, preserving hefty net interest margins—such as the KSh 104.3 billion KCB generated in just nine months of 2025.  ​Even when households and enterprises are too cash-strapped to borrow, they cannot stop transacting, and banks have mastered the art of monetizing the sheer velocity of money. Over the past decade, Kenyan lenders have aggressively expanded their non-funded income—revenue derived not from lending, but from mobile banking fees, transfer charges, account levies, loan appraisal fees, and foreign exchange spreads. For major banks, these fees now make up 30% to 40% of total operating revenue. Because more than 90% of banking transactions occur on digital channels at near-zero marginal cost to the bank, every mobile transfer or bill payment acts as a small toll collected from a captive customer base.   Moreover, the headline figures reported by Nairobi-headquartered giants are heavily cushioned by regional expansion; subsidiaries in neighboring markets like the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda now generate between 35% and half of total group profits, insulating parent companies from domestic economic sluggishness.  ​All of this unfolds within a regulatory architecture that inherently prioritizes systemic stability over consumer welfare. The Central Bank of Kenya’s primary mandate is to prevent bank failures and protect depositors' funds, and from a purely prudential standpoint, massive bank profits are viewed as a strength because they build thick capital buffers—keeping industry capital adequacy near 20%—that shield the financial system during economic storms. However, because the market is heavily concentrated in the hands of a few dominant Tier-1 banks, and because consumer-protection measures around ancillary fees, penalty charges, and transparent switching costs remain relatively weak, that systemic stability comes at a steep price to the public.
